The SMB anonymous-share fact pattern is genuinely the same contested-authorization shape as the web scenario's unauthenticated-file-exposure case (no control was ever defeated, the share simply had none), so cfaa-1030a2-misconfig's existing nuance applies as-is. The plant_marker action (writing a real 'ATTACKER WON' file via the backdoor shell, MITRE T1491.001) is tagged with cfaa-1030a2 rather than a new entry on purpose: it's part of the same single unauthorized-access event as the vsftpd backdoor that enabled it, and 1030(a)(2) already covers that access cleanly. The write itself arguably also implicates 18 U.S.C. 1030(a)(5) (knowingly causing damage/transmission), but 1030(a)(5) has its own elements (damage, loss thresholds) that this demo hasn't verified against a real source -- so per working agreement #4 we do NOT assert it on screen rather than guess. If a future legal-citation pass confirms 1030(a)(5) applies, add it then. Sourced 2026-08-23 from the same primary sources as the original entries -- see context/legal-framework.md. cfaa-1030a2.statute: 18 U.S.C. § 1030(a)(2) -- Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (federal)
cfaa-1030a2.plain_language: Intentionally accessing a computer without authorization, or exceeding authorized access, and thereby obtaining information from a protected computer. SSH credential brute-forcing (guessing a valid password) and exploiting the vsftpd backdoor (triggering a hidden, unauthorized command shell) both fit this exactly: the attacker never had valid access and circumvented a real control to get it.
elements: without authorization, or exceeding authorized access
obtaining information from a protected computer
cfaa-1030a2.penalty: Under 18 U.S.C. § 1030(c)(2): baseline misdemeanor, up to 1 year. It becomes a felony, up to 5 years, if the access was for commercial advantage or private financial gain, in furtherance of any criminal or tortious act, OR the value obtained exceeds $5,000 -- and up to 10 years on a repeat offense. Verified 2026-08-28 against the House OLRC statute text and the U.S. Sentencing Commission's 2021 Computer Crimes primer.
cfaa-1030a2.case_law: Van Buren v. United States, 141 S. Ct. 1648 (2021): the CFAA reaches accessing files/areas that are off-limits to you -- a defeated login (SQLi bypass, brute-forced SSH, a triggered backdoor shell) is squarely covered even under this narrowed reading. United States v. Morris, 928 F.2d 504 (2d Cir. 1991): the first CFAA conviction (the 'Morris Worm') -- the government need only prove intent to ACCESS without authorization, not intent to cause the damage that followed; the key precedent for holding whoever launches autonomous code liable for the access it makes.
cfaa-1030a2.evidentiary_note: The real OpenSSH auth log's failed-then-accepted password sequence, and the FTP connection log's backdoor-trigger username followed by a real shell connection, are the kind of artifacts that establish intent -- not a fat-fingered login, a deliberate exploitation sequence.

cfaa-1030a2-misconfig.statute: 18 U.S.C. § 1030(a)(2) -- Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (federal) -- unauthenticated-exposure fact pattern
cfaa-1030a2-misconfig.plain_language: Same statute as above, but the same genuinely more contested fact pattern already flagged in the web-exploit scenario: connecting to an SMB share configured for guest/anonymous access defeats no technical control -- the share simply had none. Courts have split on whether accessing a resource with no authentication barrier at all counts as 'without authorization' under the CFAA. This is deliberately the 'weakest' legal case among this scenario's findings.
elements: without authorization -- contested here, since no credential or technical barrier was ever in place
cfaa-1030a2-misconfig.penalty: Same 18 U.S.C. § 1030(c)(2) range as cfaa-1030a2 IF charged -- but prosecutorial discretion and case law both trend against charging pure unauthenticated access where no barrier was ever defeated. Present this step's exposure with less confidence than a defeated-control step.
cfaa-1030a2-misconfig.case_law: United States v. Auernheimer ('weev'), 748 F.3d 525 (3d Cir. 2014): a conviction for collecting AT&T's publicly-reachable iPad email addresses via guessable URLs was VACATED (on venue), leaving the core question -- is accessing a resource with no authentication barrier 'without authorization'? -- unresolved. Van Buren's 'gates-up-or-down' framing (141 S. Ct. 1648 (2021)) cuts toward the defense here: no gate was ever closed. Deliberately the chain's weakest legal case.
cfaa-1030a2-misconfig.evidentiary_note: The Samba connection log shows a guest/nobody-authenticated session reading a specific file -- there's no crafted payload, no bypassed check, just a connection to a share that should never have allowed anonymous access.
